facets.name: Definition
facets.description: ICD-9 482.9 denotes pneumonia attributed to bacteria when the species remains unspecified in the documented diagnosis. Infection of the pulmonary parenchyma produces alveolar inflammation and exudate, impairing ventilation and gas exchange. The bacterial attribution distinguishes this code from pneumonia with an entirely unspecified organism, while the unspecified species qualifier separates it from organism-specific bacterial pneumonia codes. Neither the distribution of an infiltrate nor antibiotic exposure alone resolves these coding distinctions.

facets.name: Symptoms
facets.description: The clinical picture includes fever or chills, cough that can produce purulent sputum, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. Examination can reveal crackles or other focal respiratory findings. Older adults and immunocompromised patients can have muted fever and instead present with new confusion, weakness, or functional decline. Symptom severity therefore requires interpretation alongside oxygenation, vital signs, and baseline health; a typical symptom cluster supports pneumonia but does not identify a bacterial species.

facets.name: Diagnosis
facets.description: Assessment integrates an acute compatible illness with a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiography or other appropriate imaging, while pulse oximetry and laboratory findings characterize physiological impact. Sputum studies and blood cultures are selected according to severity, clinical setting, and relevant risk factors rather than obtained indiscriminately. Chest CT or pleural fluid evaluation can clarify complications or an inadequate response. Negative or unavailable microbiology leaves the organism unresolved; documentation must still support bacterial pneumonia rather than infer etiology from imaging alone.

facets.name: Treatment
facets.description: Management combines antibacterial therapy with severity-guided supportive care and reassessment. Empirical antibiotic selection considers community versus hospital acquisition, comorbidities, local resistance, and risk factors for resistant pathogens; microbiological results can subsequently support narrowing therapy. Hypoxemia warrants oxygen support, and respiratory or hemodynamic instability can require hospital or intensive care. Hydration, monitoring of clinical stability, and evaluation of a poor response complement antimicrobial treatment. The code itself does not specify an antibiotic regimen or establish the site of acquisition.

facets.name: Complications
facets.description: Potential complications include worsening hypoxemia and respiratory failure, parapneumonic effusion or empyema, lung abscess, and bacteremia with systemic infection. Persistent fever, increasing oxygen requirements, or failure to improve can prompt reassessment for these complications or an alternative explanation. Pleural infection can require fluid sampling and drainage in addition to antibiotics, while respiratory failure can require ventilatory support. These events describe possible disease progression and require separate clinical documentation rather than follow automatically from the pneumonia code.

facets.name: Summary
facets.description: The profile links a documented bacterial lung infection to its respiratory presentation, imaging evidence, selectively obtained microbiology, antibacterial treatment, and severity-related complications. It preserves the distinction between a known bacterial etiology and an unidentified species, while allowing atypical presentations and incomplete microbiological confirmation. Clinical interpretation depends on the combined evidence and the recorded diagnosis; isolated symptoms, an infiltrate, or treatment with antibiotics should not independently determine the organism-specific or unspecified bacterial code.

description: Bilateral partial paralysis of vocal cords

facets.name: Definition
facets.description: ICD-9 478.33 specifies partial impairment involving both vocal cords or the larynx, preserving both the bilateral and incomplete-movement qualifiers. Neurogenic paresis can reduce opening, closure, or coordination while leaving residual movement. The resulting functional deficit depends on resting position and the muscles affected: restricted opening compromises airflow, whereas inadequate closure affects phonation and airway protection. Bilateral partial impairment therefore requires distinction from unilateral paralysis, complete bilateral immobility, and mechanically fixed vocal folds.

facets.name: Symptoms
facets.description: Voice changes include breathiness, reduced projection, vocal fatigue, and compensatory strain, but prominent dysphonia is not required when bilateral folds remain near the midline. Restricted opening can produce exertional dyspnea or inspiratory noise, while insufficient closure can cause coughing or choking during meals and an ineffective cough. The relative prominence of respiratory, voice, and swallowing symptoms reflects residual movement and glottic position. Symptom assessment should therefore cover all three functions rather than equate a relatively preserved voice with a safe airway.

facets.name: Diagnosis
facets.description: Flexible laryngoscopy assesses each fold during breathing and phonation to document bilateral reduction in movement and characterize the remaining airway. Videostroboscopy can reveal subtle vibratory or motion abnormalities, and laryngeal electromyography can support a neurogenic explanation and inform prognosis. History and targeted investigation consider neck or chest surgery, trauma, neurological disease, and lesions along the vagal or recurrent laryngeal pathways. Mechanical fixation and posterior glottic stenosis belong in the differential diagnosis; the code alone does not establish a particular cause.

facets.name: Treatment
facets.description: Management prioritizes airway adequacy while balancing voice and swallowing function. Patients with a stable airway can receive follow-up, treatment of an identifiable cause, and targeted voice or swallowing rehabilitation according to their deficits. Severe respiratory compromise can require tracheostomy, while selected persistent cases undergo an airway-enlarging procedure such as cordotomy or arytenoid surgery. These procedures can improve airflow at the expense of voice or airway protection, so intervention depends on functional assessment and recovery potential rather than on bilateral involvement alone.

facets.name: Complications
facets.description: The disease can cause upper-airway obstruction, exertional respiratory limitation, aspiration, ineffective cough, and persistent communication difficulties. The risk pattern depends on the balance between restricted opening and inadequate closure, so individual patients need not exhibit every complication. Treatment introduces additional trade-offs: airway-widening surgery can worsen voice quality, and postoperative edema, granulation tissue, fibrosis, or scarring can affect the airway or require revision. Disease-related consequences and procedure-related effects should remain distinct when interpreting a clinical record.

facets.name: Summary
facets.description: Bilateral partial vocal fold impairment is a functional laryngeal disorder whose consequences span breathing, phonation, and swallowing. A complete profile combines the bilateral movement findings, the degree of residual function, evidence for a neurogenic cause, and the functional priorities guiding management. This structure distinguishes airway-threatening restriction from primarily phonatory impairment and prevents unilateral treatment assumptions from being transferred to bilateral disease. Etiology, severity, and the need for a procedure require patient-specific evidence beyond the code label.

facets.name: Definition
facets.description: ICD-9 category 240 encompasses simple and unspecified goiter, with more specific entries distinguishing goiter described as simple from goiter left unspecified. Goiter denotes structural enlargement of the thyroid rather than a particular hormone state: the gland can be euthyroid, hypothyroid, or hyperthyroid depending on the underlying disorder. The category therefore requires separate characterization of morphology, functional status, and cause. Its use should not substitute for a more specific documented thyroid diagnosis or resolve a leaf-level coding decision.

facets.name: Symptoms
facets.description: A small goiter can remain asymptomatic and appear only as anterior neck enlargement on examination. Progressive enlargement can cause neck pressure, dysphagia, dyspnea, or positional breathing discomfort, particularly when the gland extends behind the sternum or narrows the trachea. Palpitations, heat intolerance, fatigue, or cold intolerance can accompany an underlying hormone disorder, but belong to functional assessment rather than define goiter itself. Changes in voice or rapidly evolving local symptoms warrant evaluation of structural involvement and alternative explanations.

facets.name: Diagnosis
facets.description: Evaluation documents the size, distribution, and compressive effects of thyroid enlargement and checks thyroid function, commonly beginning with TSH and appropriate thyroid hormone measurements. Ultrasound characterizes gland structure and any nodules; antibody testing addresses a suspected autoimmune cause. Radionuclide assessment is selected according to functional findings, while fine-needle aspiration targets nodules meeting appropriate clinical and ultrasound criteria. Distinguishing diffuse enlargement from nodular disease and structural compression from hormone-related symptoms provides the detail absent from the category label.

facets.name: Treatment
facets.description: Management follows the demonstrated cause and consequences of enlargement. Stable, asymptomatic enlargement with reassuring evaluation can be observed with clinical and biochemical follow-up. Confirmed iodine deficiency or hypothyroidism requires appropriate cause-directed treatment, while nodules and autonomous function follow their own evaluation pathways. Compressive symptoms, substernal extension, or concerning structural findings can prompt surgical assessment. Routine thyroid hormone suppression is not a universal treatment for euthyroid goiter, and neither antithyroid medication nor surgery follows automatically from the code.

facets.name: Complications
facets.description: Large or substernal goiters can compress the trachea or esophagus, producing airway limitation or dysphagia. Progression of the underlying thyroid disorder can alter hormone function, while a nodule can require a separate malignancy assessment based on its own features. If surgery becomes necessary, potential complications include bleeding, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, and hypoparathyroidism. The clinical profile keeps effects of gland enlargement, consequences of the underlying disease, and treatment-related risks separate rather than attributing them all to uncomplicated goiter.

facets.name: Summary
facets.description: A complete goiter profile combines structural enlargement, thyroid hormone status, underlying cause, and the presence or absence of local compression. This distinction supports selective testing and separates an observation pathway from treatment of a functional disorder or surgical management of compressive disease. ICD-9 240 is a category-level entry; the final code should reflect available diagnostic specificity, including the applicable child code. Enlargement alone does not establish thyroid toxicity, hypothyroidism, a particular nodule subtype, or malignancy.

facets.name: Definition
facets.description: ICD-9 428.0 denotes congestive heart failure without a specified subtype in the code. Congestion reflects increased cardiac filling pressures and fluid accumulation, while impaired systemic perfusion can coexist to varying degrees. The syndrome can arise from reduced systolic function, abnormal ventricular filling, or mixed mechanisms. The unspecified designation preserves uncertainty about ejection-fraction phenotype and does not establish acute, chronic, or acute-on-chronic disease. These distinctions require the clinical assessment and diagnostic wording rather than extrapolation from edema or medication use.

facets.name: Symptoms
facets.description: Pulmonary congestion can produce exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, cough, and difficulty sleeping flat, while systemic venous congestion can cause dependent edema, abdominal fullness, and weight gain. Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance reflect the combined effects of circulatory impairment and congestion. Examination can identify lung crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, or peripheral edema, but findings vary with disease distribution and treatment. New or rapidly worsening symptoms should be interpreted with the clinical course to distinguish deterioration from a stable baseline.

facets.name: Diagnosis
facets.description: Diagnosis integrates symptoms and signs with objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction or elevated filling pressures. BNP or NT-proBNP measurements can support assessment, and echocardiography evaluates ejection fraction, chamber structure, valves, and relevant functional abnormalities. ECG, chest imaging, renal function, and other laboratory tests characterize associated disease and treatment constraints. Evaluation also addresses precipitating or alternative causes of dyspnea and edema. An unspecified CHF code does not replace this phenotyping, and a reduced ejection fraction or a specific acuity should be assigned only when supported.

facets.name: Treatment
facets.description: Treatment separates relief of congestion from therapies directed at the established heart failure phenotype and underlying disease. Diuretics address fluid overload; patients with confirmed HFrEF can receive appropriate renin-angiotensin system treatment, evidence-based beta blockade, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor as tolerated. Selection and adjustment account for blood pressure, renal function, electrolytes, and clinical stability. Other phenotypes and selected device indications require their own assessment. The unspecified code therefore supports a management context rather than a universal medication or device regimen.

facets.name: Complications
facets.description: Decompensation can cause pulmonary edema, respiratory compromise, recurrent hospitalization, and worsening functional capacity. Reduced perfusion and venous congestion can contribute to kidney or liver injury, while underlying cardiac disease can increase the risk of arrhythmia and sudden death. Advanced cases can require assessment for mechanical circulatory support or transplantation. Treatment also requires surveillance for hypotension, renal deterioration, and electrolyte abnormalities. The profile distinguishes disease progression from medication-related effects and does not presume that every patient with 428.0 has advanced or acutely decompensated disease.

facets.name: Summary
facets.description: The profile connects pulmonary and systemic congestion, objective cardiac evaluation, phenotype-dependent treatment, and potential organ complications while retaining the diagnostic limits of an unspecified CHF code. It identifies the information needed to move from a broad syndrome label to a more specific description of function and acuity. Symptoms and medication patterns can contribute clinical context, but the documented diagnosis and supporting investigation determine whether systolic, diastolic, acute, chronic, or other more specific coding categories apply.

facets.name: Definition
facets.description: ICD-9 493.90 refers to asthma with unspecified type and without a stated acute exacerbation or status asthmaticus in this code. Asthma combines variable respiratory symptoms with variable expiratory airflow limitation, commonly in a background of airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness. The label does not identify an allergic mechanism, a severity class, or current control. It also does not establish the absence of symptoms; specifying an acute complication requires its own clinical evidence and diagnostic documentation.

facets.name: Symptoms
facets.description: Wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea typically vary in intensity and timing, with nocturnal or early-morning symptoms and episodes related to exercise, allergens, smoke, or respiratory infection. Symptom-free intervals can alternate with periods of deterioration. The clinical profile records both the symptom pattern and its functional impact, including sleep disturbance, activity limitation, and increased need for relief. Individual symptoms overlap with other respiratory disorders, so their temporal variability and relation to objective airflow changes help organize the evidence.

facets.name: Diagnosis
facets.description: Assessment seeks a compatible variable symptom history together with objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation. Spirometry before and after bronchodilator treatment can demonstrate reversibility; repeated testing, peak-flow variability, or selected challenge testing can help when initial spirometry is nondiagnostic. Evaluation considers alternative explanations and comorbid conditions that affect breathing or symptom perception. Establishing asthma, characterizing its control, and identifying an acute episode are related but distinct tasks. Normal testing at one visit can require reassessment rather than settle a variable disease presentation.

facets.name: Treatment
facets.description: Management uses an age-appropriate inhaled corticosteroid-containing strategy to address airway inflammation, with reliever treatment selected within the prescribed regimen. Review of inhaler technique, adherence, exposure to triggers, and relevant comorbidities accompanies medication adjustment. A written action plan links changes in symptoms or lung function to a response pathway and thresholds for seeking care. Persistent poor control prompts reassessment of diagnosis and contributing factors. Specific drug combinations and treatment intensity depend on the clinical assessment rather than follow from the unspecified ICD code.

facets.name: Complications
facets.description: Uncontrolled disease can cause recurrent exacerbations, sleep disruption, exercise limitation, and repeated urgent-care or hospital visits. A severe attack can progress to marked airflow obstruction, hypoxemia, and respiratory failure. Previous serious attacks and the current control pattern contribute to assessment of future risk, while adverse effects depend on the treatment actually used. These possible complications should be distinguished from the qualifier assigned to a particular encounter: their presence in a general disease profile does not establish an exacerbation or status asthmaticus in the record.

facets.name: Summary
facets.description: The profile connects variable symptoms, objective lung-function evidence, inflammatory control, reliever use, and future attack risk while retaining the unspecified diagnostic qualifiers of 493.90. It separates confirmation of the disease from assessment of current control and documentation of an acute complication. This organization supports interpretation of dispersed respiratory evidence without inferring severity, an allergic subtype, exacerbation, or status asthmaticus from a single symptom, inhaler prescription, or historical mention of an attack.
